sermons.life_context: He was still a doctoral student in systematic theology at Boston University, married to Coretta Scott since June 1953, and had served as associate minister at Ebenezer in Atlanta during breaks. Dexter called him on 7 March 1954, and he accepted on 14 April.

Still a doctoral student at Boston University and married to Coretta Scott since June 1953, he had preached his trial sermon at Dexter in Montgomery the previous month; the church would call him a week later, on 7 March 1954. This guest sermon came during a Michigan visit that also included an address to the Lansing NAACP.

He was pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery and, as president of the Montgomery Improvement Association, was leading the city's bus boycott, which was still under way. His home had been bombed that January, with his family unharmed; his first child, Yolanda, had been born in November 1955.

He was pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery and president of the Montgomery Improvement Association, whose bus boycott was still continuing; it ended the next month, and on 21 December 1956 he rode an integrated bus. His home had been bombed in January 1956, with his family unharmed.

Pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery, he had seen the bus boycott end in December 1956, and in January 1957 became leader of the body soon renamed the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. He and Coretta Scott King had travelled to Ghana for its independence, 4–12 March 1957, on a trip funded by the Montgomery Improvement Association and Dexter.

He was pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery and, since January 1957, leader of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. His son Martin Luther King III had been born on 23 October 1957, and a week before this sermon he had given a similar version at Howard University's School of Religion convocation in Washington, D.C.

Since February 1960 he had lived in Atlanta as co-pastor of Ebenezer with his father and as president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, and he took part in the 1961–1962 Albany, Georgia, campaign; his son Dexter was born in January 1961. According to the King Papers, he had orchestrated the letter-writing campaign urging West Hunter to call Ralph Abernathy, whose installation this was.

He was based in Atlanta as co-pastor of Ebenezer with his father and president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. That summer he had been arrested for a third time in Albany, Georgia, on 27 July 1962, and while in jail worked on sermon drafts later published in Strength to Love.

The 1963 text is the Strength to Love chapter he revised between July 1962 and March 1963, while co-pastor of Ebenezer in Atlanta and president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. In that period he was jailed in Albany, Georgia, where he worked on sermon drafts later published in the book, and his daughter Bernice was born in March 1963.

The 1963 text is the Strength to Love chapter he drafted between July 1962 and March 1963, while co-pastor of Ebenezer in Atlanta and president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference; in summer 1962 he was jailed in Albany, Georgia, where he worked on sermon drafts for the book. Its draft title links it to 'The Mastery of Fear', preached at Dexter on 21 July 1957.

He was co-pastor of Ebenezer in Atlanta and president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. Earlier in 1963, during the Birmingham campaign, he had been arrested on Good Friday and written 'Letter from Birmingham Jail', and on 28 August he delivered 'I Have a Dream' at the March on Washington, three weeks before this funeral.

Still co-pastor of Ebenezer in Atlanta and president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, he had moved into a Chicago apartment in January 1966 when the SCLC began its campaign against poor housing there. In April 1967 he had publicly opposed the Vietnam War in his Riverside Church address.

He was preaching at Ebenezer, where he was co-pastor with his father, while leading the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. He had opposed the Vietnam War in his April 1967 Riverside Church address and announced the Poor People's Campaign in December 1967. He was killed in Memphis two months later.

Co-pastor of Ebenezer in Atlanta and president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, he had announced the Poor People's Campaign in December 1967 and was supporting striking sanitation workers in Memphis, where a 28 March march had ended in violence. He had publicly opposed the Vietnam War in his April 1967 Riverside Church address. He was killed four days later.

Co-pastor of Ebenezer in Atlanta and president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, he had announced the Poor People's Campaign in December 1967. He was in Memphis supporting striking sanitation workers, having returned after a 28 March march ended in violence to restore nonviolence to the movement. He was shot at the Lorraine Motel the next day.
